finalMessage:
## Final verdict: CONCEDE-WITH-CHANGES

The reversal is reasonable and better matches the owner’s intended product. Academy Brain should become an internally owned part of CourseDeveloperStudio’s repository and product release while remaining Python.

The important qualification is:

> “Built into Studio” should mean one product, one source repository, one coordinated release, one user experience, and one support responsibility—not one programming language, one executable, or necessarily one container.

Moving the files alone would not satisfy the owner. Studio must actually let users start generation, monitor it, cancel it, and receive the finished material without knowing Academy Brain exists separately.

## 1. Does the proposal satisfy the owner?

Yes, provided all of the following are true:

- Academy Brain’s authoritative source moves into the Studio repository.
- The old Academy Brain repository stops being an independently developed product.
- A Studio release includes a tested Academy Brain revision automatically.
- Users operate it entirely through the Studio interface.
- The same team owns failures across the UI, API, job worker, and Python engine.
- There is one coordinated installation/update procedure.

There would be a gap if “move into Studio” meant merely copying the Python folder while:

- generation still requires manually launching scripts;
- the old repository remains the real source of truth;
- Studio and Academy Brain must be upgraded separately;
- outputs remain on a worker’s local disk;
- failures are visible only in Python logs;
- or users must understand which underlying component is responsible.

The owner is describing a product boundary, not a process boundary. A separate background process is invisible to him and does not contradict his request.

## 2. Recommended concrete repository and deployment shape

Use a monorepo with the Academy Brain name preserved. `/academy-brain` is clearer than `/worker`, because the engine is more than a single executable: it includes contracts, gates, templates, prompts, scaffolding, and tests.

```text
CourseDeveloperStudio/
├── frontend/                         # Next.js application
│   ├── src/
│   └── Dockerfile
│
├── backend/
│   ├── CourseDeveloper.sln
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── CourseDeveloper.Core/
│   │   ├── CourseDeveloper.Infrastructure/
│   │   ├── CourseDeveloper.Api/
│   │   └── CourseDeveloper.Worker/  # durable job consumer
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── Dockerfile.api
│   └── Dockerfile.worker
│
├── academy-brain/                    # authoritative Python engine source
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   ├── scripts/swarm/
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── 00-contracts/
│   ├── 75-bundle/
│   ├── 80-generation/
│   └── required templates/prompts/
│
├── contracts/
│   └── generation-job/               # request/result/event schemas
│       ├── request.schema.json
│       ├── result.schema.json
│       └── fixtures/
│
├── database/
│   └── migrations/
│
├── deploy/
│   ├── compose.yaml                  # local/integrated deployment
│   └── production manifests/
│
└── tests/
    └── integration/                  # .NET ↔ Python contract/E2E tests
```

The production release would contain at least three running services:

1. Next.js frontend.
2. .NET API.
3. Dedicated generation worker.

The worker image should contain both:

- `CourseDeveloper.Worker`;
- the Python runtime and the Academy Brain code from the same repository commit.

The flow remains:

```text
Studio UI
  → .NET API
  → GenerationJob in Postgres
  → CourseDeveloper.Worker
  → local Academy Brain Python subprocess
  → durable artifact storage
  → job result/status in Postgres
  → Studio UI
```

That is one product release with multiple internal processes. It is the same pattern as a hospital system containing a web portal, database, and report processor: multiple internal pieces, but one system to its owner.

Course inputs, temporary workspaces, generated PDFs, credentials, and customer data should not live in the source repository. They remain in isolated runtime workspaces, secret storage, and durable artifact storage.

The existing Studio repository currently has separate frontend and API container definitions, but no repository-level deployment manifest or worker image, so “one deployment unit” does not exist yet: [README.md](</D:/vault/SM/CourseDeveloperStudio/README.md:24>), [backend Dockerfile](</D:/vault/SM/CourseDeveloperStudio/backend/Dockerfile:1>), [frontend Dockerfile](</D:/vault/SM/CourseDeveloperStudio/frontend/Dockerfile:1>).

### Migration rule

Do not maintain both repositories after the move.

- Preserve Academy Brain’s useful Git history when importing it if practical.
- Declare the Studio monorepo authoritative at a specific cutover commit.
- Archive the old repository as read-only.
- Do not sync changes in both directions.
- Do not retain a submodule or package reference back to the old release.

Otherwise the original “two drifting copies” risk returns under a different name.

## 3. Effect on Decisions 2, 7, and 9

### Decision 2: ownership, versioning, and contract tests — must be rewritten

The old decision no longer applies as written.

Remove:

- separate Academy Brain product ownership;
- independently published Academy Brain releases;
- Studio pinning an external engine version;
- cross-team ownership of the contract;
- compatibility testing against separately released engine versions.

Replace it with:

> Academy Brain is an internal Python component of CourseDeveloperStudio. The Studio team owns the UI, API, durable job system, Python engine, integration contract, deployment, monitoring, and upgrades as one product. The engine and its caller are released from the same repository commit.

Contract tests should absolutely remain. Repository co-location does not remove process boundaries, JSON parsing, exit codes, cancellation, or crash behavior. It merely turns the contract into an internal compatibility boundary owned by one team.

Keep a `contractVersion` in job payloads because:

- queued jobs can survive a deployment;
- a worker may pick up a job created by the preceding release;
- rolling deployments can briefly run adjacent builds;
- old job records must remain understandable.

But record the Studio build/commit that executed a job, rather than an independently pinned Academy Brain release number.

### Decision 7: GenerationJob and dedicated worker — still holds

This decision remains architecturally correct:

- durable Postgres job and event records;
- a worker independent from the API lifecycle;
- atomic job claims and leases;
- heartbeat and crash recovery;
- idempotency;
- cancellation;
- retry policy;
- per-course concurrency control;
- no Redis or RabbitMQ initially.

Co-location does not make long-running generation safe inside an HTTP request. Academy Brain already has filesystem locks and resumable external task state, confirming that generation has a durable lifecycle rather than a normal request/response lifecycle.

One wording change is needed: the worker is “separately running/deployable within the Studio product,” not an independently versioned product.

I would retain the .NET worker as the job supervisor and have it launch the bundled Python engine. That preserves the already-designed job infrastructure and keeps Academy Brain focused on generation. Replacing it with a Python process that also owns database polling is possible, but it expands the reversal unnecessarily.

### Decision 9: runtime, secrets, workspace, and artifacts — still holds unchanged

If anything, this becomes more important. “Part of Studio” means Studio inherits full responsibility for:

- a reproducible Python runtime;
- declared dependencies;
- NotebookLM credential storage and rotation;
- organization-specific credential policy;
- isolated job workspaces;
- cleanup and retention;
- durable output storage;
- hashes and artifact locations;
- resumable external task identifiers;
- crash recovery;
- monitoring and support.

The current Python project still does not declare NotebookLM in `pyproject.toml`, despite live generation depending on it: [pyproject.toml](</D:/vault/academy-brain/pyproject.toml:1>). And the engine documentation confirms that the filesystem, staged evidence, gates, and generated artifacts are substantial parts of the engine—not incidental scripts: [ENGINE.md](</D:/vault/academy-brain/docs/ENGINE.md:9>).

“Same deployment” must not be interpreted as putting generation inside the API container. The API should remain responsive even if a generation job takes an hour, crashes, or exhausts memory.

## 4. Risks to explain to the owner

I would tell him this:

> We can make Academy Brain a real built-in part of Studio. You will have one product to install, update, and use. You will not see or manage a separate Academy Brain product.
>
> Behind the screen, the heavy course-generation work still needs its own background runner, just as a laboratory analyzer works behind the pharmacy system. That is necessary so the Studio website does not freeze or lose a course when generation takes a long time.
>
> The main tradeoff is that Studio now takes full responsibility for Academy Brain. A change to the engine can affect the whole product, releases may take more testing, and the server must support both .NET and Python. But there will be no separate version for you to select or maintain.
>
> During the move, we must ensure we do not accidentally create two Academy Brains. Once the code is moved, the old repository will be archived and the Studio copy will become the only official one.

The genuine risks are:

- A larger combined release requires broader testing.
- The worker host must support both .NET and Python.
- Python dependencies can enlarge the worker image and security-update surface.
- A broken engine change can now block the overall Studio release.
- Repository permissions become shared; anyone able to modify Studio may potentially modify the engine.
- Moving only code, while omitting contracts, templates, prompts, or required assets, could produce something called Academy Brain that is not actually the same engine.
- Keeping the old repository active would create two competing “official” versions.

These are manageable and do not outweigh the owner’s expressed preference.

## 5. Ruling

**CONCEDE-WITH-CHANGES.**

Approve the reversal, but formalize it as:

> Academy Brain becomes an internally owned Python component of the CourseDeveloperStudio monorepo and coordinated Studio release. It executes through a dedicated durable worker, but it is not separately versioned, independently deployed, or maintained as an external product. Studio users access and manage generation entirely through Studio.

Before implementation, the binding vision and ticket must be amended explicitly. The current documents still prohibit copying Academy Brain into Studio, require a pinned external release, and describe separate ownership: [integration ticket](</D:/vault/SM/CourseDeveloperStudio/docs/tickets/2026-09-04-academy-brain-mvp-integration.md:162>) and [vision constraint](</D:/vault/SM/CourseDeveloperStudio/docs/tickets/2026-09-04-academy-brain-mvp-integration-vision.md:11>). Leaving those instructions active would make subsequent implementation agents simultaneously required to follow contradictory decisions.

No files were edited.
